catalog_quote: [p. 51] a. There are three pitch levels: high, mid, and low. b. There are five possible patterns in a word: high throughout: pélɛ 'also'; mid throughout: pɛlɛ 'to start'; low throughout: pɛ̀lɛ 'small'; high to low: -pɛ̂rɛ 'side (of the body)'; mid to high-low: pɔmûŋ 'germinate'. c. Words with high, high-low, and low tone patterns have stress on the initial syllable. Mid-high-low have stress on the second vowel, since this stress is automatic and does not differentiate one word from another (as English stress does in 'progress' as a noun and 'progress' as a verb). In the area around Gbarnga, /k/, /g/, and, most frequently /ɣ/ are not pronounced when they are in an unstressed syllable between two front vowels. ... e. The patterns presented apply to words without prefixes or suffixes. Affixes carry their own tone patterns. [p. 190] 2. Stress. While stress is generally non-contrastive in Mande it is generally distinctive. In Kpelle, it falls on the first high-toned syllable in the word, or if the word has no high tones, it falls on the first syllable. Stress is acoustically marked by an increase in the loudness of the syllable and is often accompanied by a slight increase in the length of the syllable. [SPA 1979 digest of Welmers 1962: 86] STRESS: "Stress...is non-phonemic...conditioned by tone." Stress always occurs with the first /high/, or /low/, tone of a word. Stress never occurs with /mid/ tone. (p. 86)

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kpelle is a three-level tone language (high, mid, low) in which stress is automatic and non-contrastive, predictable from the word's tone pattern: it falls on the first high-toned syllable of the word; in words with no high tone (low-throughout words per p. 51; 'no high tones' per p. 190) it falls on the first syllable. Under the five-pattern analysis of p. 51 this puts stress on the initial syllable for H, HL and L words and on the second vowel for the mid-high-low pattern. Correlates: loudness plus slight lengthening. Welmers 1962: 86 (as digested by the Stanford Phonology Archive 1979) says the same in toneme terms: stress is non-phonemic, conditioned by tone, always with the first high or low tone of the word and never with mid.
new_statements.exceptions: Mid-high-low words stress the second vowel (p. 51). The two pages disagree on all-mid words: p. 190 gives first syllable when there is no high tone, whereas Welmers 1962: 86 (via SPA 1979) says stress never occurs with mid tone. In the Gbarnga area /k/, /g/ and especially /ɣ/ are not pronounced in an unstressed syllable between two front vowels (p. 51). Sinclair 1968: xxiv (pedagogical) instead says syllables receive equal stress with slight extra stress on a falling-tone syllable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; p. 51e states the tone patterns 'apply to words without prefixes or suffixes', affixes carrying their own tone patterns. Stress is explicitly automatic and non-distinctive; the language is tonal.
new_statements.identity_note: Thach & Dwyer 1981 describes Liberian Kpelle as taught to Peace Corps volunteers (Totota Lutheran orthography, Bong County; dialect notes for Gbarnga, Totota, Jorquellie), i.e. libe1247. The Konoshenko 2017 Jazyki mira chapter already held by the project under guin1254 states that phonological stress is absent, but explicitly for central Guinean Kpelle (Hɔŋkwele variety, Nzérékoré) = guin1254, a different glottocode; do not transfer that statement to libe1247. Welmers 1962 (Liberian Kpelle, SPA digest p. 86) agrees with the handbook that stress is non-phonemic and tone-conditioned.

tone_statements.quote: As in most sub-Saharan African languages, tone is both lexically and grammatically significant in Kpelle. Welmers (1973) described three distinct levels of tone for Kpelle: high, mid, and low, and a falling glide on single syllable words. This is borne out by the production of the informant for this dictionary, except that the falling glide occurs also in polysyllabic words. In this work, the mid tones are left unmarked, high tones are marked / ´/, low / `/, and the falling glide, /^/.
